intro: To compare two Word documents on a Mac, open Word and go to Review > Compare > Compare Documents. Pick the original file and the revised file, then click OK. Word leaves both files alone and builds a new copy with every difference marked as a tracked change.
tldr: Compare builds a new tracked copy. Your original file stays unchanged.
The Original box must hold the unedited version you sent out, not the last round.
Untick Formatting under More >> when you want a text-first redline.
Track Changes turned on from the start beats any comparison you run later.
Combine Documents merges several reviewers' copies, two documents per run.

blocks.text: Compare two Word documents on a Mac, step by step

Start with both files saved on your Mac. Keep the sent copy and the returned copy as separate files. Open Word, then go to Review > Compare > Compare Documents. A dialog opens with two boxes, Original and Revised. Each box takes a file you pick from a list or browse for.

items: Save the sent copy and the returned copy as separate files on your Mac.
Open Word and choose Review > Compare > Compare Documents.
In the Original box, pick the unedited version you sent out.
In the Revised box, pick the version that came back.
Click More >> and untick Formatting if you want to see text changes only.
Click OK. Word opens a new document with the differences marked.

blocks.title: Menu names differ by version
blocks.text: Microsoft's compare support page is labeled for Word 2019 for Mac. That page shows Tools > Track Changes > Compare Documents, while third-party guides show Review > Compare. If your menu does not match, look under both. This guide could not confirm the exact path for the newest Word for Mac release, so check your own menu bar.
Why the Original box matters most

Compare reads two files and reports what changed from the first to the second. Swap the boxes and the report flips. Insertions look like deletions, and a deleted clause looks like new text. Your reader then sees the opposite of what happened. Put the unedited sent-out file in Original every time.
A worked example with a returned contract

Say you sent a services agreement out on a Monday. It comes back on a Thursday with tracked edits. Meanwhile, someone on your team saved a working copy on Tuesday and changed a payment clause. If you compare the Thursday file against that Tuesday copy, the redline hides the Tuesday change. Compare against the Monday file you actually sent. The Tuesday change then shows up as a real change, and you can decide what to do with it.
Compare options in the More window

Under More >> you find extra checkboxes. The table below uses the option names from CustomGuide's Windows walkthrough. Mac menus may use slightly different labels, so match them by name and by meaning.

rows: Marks bold, italic, and underline changes
Untick if old comments are noise
Keep on when defined terms matter
Compares by character or by word
Use word level for clean legal text
Puts results in the original, revised, or a new document
Pick a new document for a fresh copy
blocks.caption: Compare options as listed in CustomGuide's Windows steps.

blocks.text: Why your redline looks noisy

Most noisy redlines come from formatting. Font swaps, spacing fixes, and style changes show up as edits. Real legal changes then get buried in the noise. Untick Formatting to see the text changes first. Run a second compare with formatting on only when formatting matters for the job.

Track Changes matters too. If it was off while people edited, Compare has to rebuild the edits after the fact. The Journal of Accountancy article calls comparison a narrow fallback for that case. Treat it as a rescue, not a habit.
Combine Documents when several people reviewed

Compare handles two files at a time. When three people marked up the same contract, use Review > Compare > Combine Documents instead. Combine also works on two documents per run. Microsoft says the Original should be the unedited version that went out for review. Label unmarked changes so each reviewer's edits carry a name.

items: Set the Original to the unedited version you sent out.
Set the Revised to the first reviewer's copy.
Turn on Label unmarked changes with, then type the reviewer's name.
Keep the first merge set to show changes in a New document.
Save the merged file, make it the Original, and combine the next reviewer's copy as the Revised document.

blocks.text: Metadata and what it means for your redline

Metadata is information stored inside a file that you do not see on the page. It can include author names, timestamps, and edits from earlier drafts. A redline does not remove it. Before you send a compared file outside your firm, follow your firm's review steps. Your employer's rules on client data come first, every time.

blocks.title: One state's rule, not a national one
blocks.text: A North Carolina ethics opinion says a lawyer may not search for confidential metadata. If a lawyer views it by accident, the lawyer must notify the sender and may not use the information without consent. Check your own state's rules and your firm's policy before you rely on this.
Dedicated compare tools: check Mac support first

Some teams buy a dedicated comparison tool. Litera's Compare product page names only Windows for its desktop product. It says nothing about macOS, system requirements, or price. Draftable's legal page says you can compare from Microsoft Office and Outlook, and it lists Word. It does not state macOS support. Ask each vendor for Mac support in writing, and check their pricing pages before you buy.
Mistakes that waste the most time

items: Comparing against a copy that someone already edited.
Leaving Track Changes off while you edit your own draft.
Swapping Original and Revised, then reading the output as the truth.
Keeping Formatting on for a text-only review.
Assuming a Mac menu matches a guide written for Windows.
Sending a compared file without checking your firm's data rules.

blocks.text: What to do when the redline still looks wrong

Start with the two file names in the dialog. Confirm which one is Original. Then check the More >> options. If the redline still looks off, open the sent copy from your sent folder and compare again. Read the result section by section. Headings, numbering, and tables often change together, so one missed heading can hide a block of edits.

faq.question: Can I compare two Word documents on a Mac without buying anything extra?
faq.answer: Compare is built into Word for Mac, so you do not need an add-on. You still need a working copy of Word for Mac. This guide did not check Microsoft's licensing terms, so confirm your plan includes Word before you rely on the steps.

faq.question: Why does Compare mark almost my whole document as changed?
faq.answer: Usually the boxes are swapped, the Original is not the version that went out, or formatting differs across the files. Check the file names, untick Formatting under More >>, and compare again. A large rewrite in the returned copy can also cause this.

faq.question: What is the difference between Compare and Combine?
faq.answer: Compare takes two files and produces one revised copy with the differences marked. Combine merges the revisions from two documents and can label each reviewer's unmarked changes. Use Combine when several people reviewed the same draft.

faq.question: Does Compare change my original file?
faq.answer: No. Microsoft's support page says Word creates a new copy based on the Original. The Original stays unchanged, so keep the sent version safe in its own folder.

faq.question: Does Word for the web have the same Compare command?
faq.answer: This guide did not confirm it from a Microsoft page. Use Word for Mac for the steps here, and check your own version before you plan a review around it.

faq.question: Can Lazur run the comparison for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur points at the controls, explains what you see, and guides you one click at a time. It does not click buttons or edit files for you, so you run the comparison yourself.

faq.question: What should I do if a returned file has hidden data in it?
faq.answer: Follow your firm's rules and your state's ethics rules. The North Carolina opinion says not to search for confidential metadata, and to notify the sender if you see it by accident. Ask your ethics counsel or supervisor when the rule is unclear.

costs.title: Hours spent rechecking a bad redline
costs.text: A comparison against the wrong base file gives a redline that looks clean and hides real edits. You then reread the whole document to be safe. Nobody has measured how long redlining takes lawyers, so no study gives a clean number. The closest figure is the median lawyer pay of $159,670 in May 2025. That works out to about $77 an hour on a 2,080-hour year. That is our arithmetic, not a Bureau of Labor Statistics figure, and it covers all lawyers, not only redliners.

costs.title: Edits that never reach your screen
costs.text: The bigger cost is a change you never see. A clause moves, or a number changes, and the compare misses it. The error then carries into the next draft and into the signed version. Track Changes left off from the start is the usual cause. Compare can recover some edits afterward, but it is a fallback, not a replacement for tracked edits.

costs.title: Hidden data in the file you send
costs.text: Redlines can carry metadata from earlier drafts, including author names and timestamps. A North Carolina ethics opinion says a lawyer may not search for confidential metadata. If a lawyer sees it by accident, the lawyer must notify the sender. That is one state's rule, not a national one, but it shows the risk. Clean handling of files is a cost you pay in time, not only in risk.

costs.title: Long review nights on top of heavy work
costs.text: A 2026 study in the Journal of Affective Disorders found nearly half of working lawyers reported high or very high burnout. The study covers all lawyers and does not measure redlining, so it cannot say comparison work causes burnout. It does show how much pressure already sits on lawyers, which makes avoidable manual checking more costly.

causes.title: Track Changes was off from the start
causes.text: If nobody turned on Track Changes before editing, the edits are not tracked. Compare then has to rebuild them from two files. The Journal of Accountancy article calls comparison a narrow fallback for that case, so a clean redline is not guaranteed.

causes.title: Formatting differences flood the result
causes.text: Bold, italic, and underline changes and font swaps show up as edits. Each one adds noise. Real legal changes get harder to find, and reviewers start skimming. Formatting is a common reason a redline looks busier than it should.

causes.title: The base file was already edited
causes.text: This is the most expensive cause. If the Original is not the version that went out, the redline shows the wrong changes. Edits made in your working copy look like they came from the other side. Teams often do this without noticing, because the file names look alike.

causes.title: Menu paths differ between guides
causes.text: Microsoft's Word 2019 for Mac page shows Tools > Track Changes > Compare Documents. Third-party guides show Review > Compare. A reader who follows the wrong guide may not find the command. Check your own menu bar before you follow any written path.

causes.title: Hidden data travels with the file
causes.text: Metadata and earlier draft text can sit inside a file you send. A redline does not clear it. People usually notice only when someone else finds it. The cause is a workflow gap, not a single Word setting, so the fix is a habit and a checklist.

fixes.title: Turn on Track Changes before you edit
fixes.text: Open the working copy in Word and go to Review > Track Changes. Turn it on before anyone edits the text. In recent Word for Mac releases, ⌘⇧E also toggles it. If that key does nothing on your version, use the Review tab. Keep it on until the document is final, so every change shows up without a compare step.

fixes.title: Untick Formatting in the Compare window
fixes.text: Open Compare Documents, click More >>, and untick Formatting. Word then ignores changes to bold, italics, and underlines. Use this for a text-first review. Keep Formatting on when font or style changes matter, such as a required filing format. Run that check as a second pass, not as the first one.

fixes.title: Set Original and Revised in the right boxes
fixes.text: Original is the unedited version you sent out. Revised is the version that came back. Before you click OK, read both file names in the dialog. A swap makes insertions look like deletions, and the redline reads backwards. Name your files with dates so the right one is easy to spot.

fixes.title: Use Combine Documents for several reviewers
fixes.text: Go to Review > Compare > Combine Documents. Set Original to the unedited sent copy and Revised to the first reviewer's copy. Turn on Label unmarked changes with and type the reviewer's name. Save the merged file, make it the Original, and combine the next copy as Revised. Combine takes two documents at a time, so repeat this for each reviewer.

fixes.title: Check which version is the base
fixes.text: Before you compare, ask what the other side started from. If a colleague edited your copy after it went out, do not use that copy as Original. Compare against the file that left your office. Write the base file's name in your matter notes so the next person uses the same one.

fixes.title: Read the redline by section
fixes.text: Do not trust a quick scroll. Go section by section and check headings, numbering, defined terms, and tables. Look for whole blocks marked as changed, since a moved paragraph can show up as a delete and an insert. Read your cover email against the redline before you send anything.

fixes.title: Follow your firm's metadata rules
fixes.text: Do not search a file for metadata you were not sent to review. If you see hidden data by accident, stop and follow your state's rule. The North Carolina opinion says to notify the sender and not use the information without consent. Ask your ethics counsel or supervisor when the rule is unclear.

fixes.title: Check Mac support before you buy a tool
fixes.text: Litera's product page names only Windows for its desktop product. Draftable's legal page lists Word but does not state macOS support. Before you buy, ask each vendor for Mac support, the Word versions they support, and current pricing. Do not assume a Windows feature works the same way on your Mac.

plan.label: Day 1
plan.title: Save the sent version
plan.text: Save the file you sent as a read-only copy in its own folder. Name it with the send date. Do not edit it after it leaves your desk. This file becomes your Original for every comparison.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: Turn on Track Changes
plan.text: Open the working copy and turn on Track Changes before you touch the text. Check the Review tab to confirm it is on. Keep it on until the document is final.

plan.label: On return
plan.title: Compare the returned file
plan.text: When the returned copy arrives, open Review > Compare > Compare Documents. Set Original to the sent copy and Revised to the returned copy. Untick Formatting under More >> for a text-first pass.

plan.label: Review pass
plan.title: Read the result by section
plan.text: Scroll section by section. Check headings, numbering, defined terms, and tables. Ask Lazur to explain any change you do not understand, while the document stays open on screen.

plan.label: Several reviewers
plan.title: Combine the copies
plan.text: If more people reviewed, use Review > Compare > Combine Documents. Label each reviewer's unmarked changes with a name. Make each merged file the next Original.

plan.label: Before sending
plan.title: Check data rules first
plan.text: Confirm your firm's rules on client data and metadata before the compared file leaves the firm. If the rules are unclear, ask your supervisor or ethics counsel before you send.
